report:
## Conclusion

Yes — strong randomized-trial evidence shows that regular low-dose CT (LDCT) screening reduces lung cancer mortality among heavy current or former smokers.

The U.S. **National Lung Screening Trial (NLST)**, which enrolled over 53,000 heavy smokers/ex-smokers, found that three annual LDCT screens reduced lung cancer–specific mortality by 20% compared with chest X-ray, and reduced all-cause mortality by 7% (https://www.cancer.gov/types/lung/research/nlst; https://www.atsjournals.org/doi/full/10.1164/rccm.201705-0914OC?cookieSet=1).

The European **NELSON trial**, involving nearly 16,000 heavy smokers randomized to volume-based LDCT screening versus no screening, confirmed and extended these findings: lung cancer mortality was about 24% lower in screened men and 33% lower in screened women after 10 years of follow-up (https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793?cookieSet=1). A synthesis of this and related trial evidence (German Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care, IQWiG/Gesundheitsinformation.de) similarly concludes that "systematic lung cancer screening with low-dose CT lowers mortality from lung cancer in (current or former) heavy smokers," while cautioning that this benefit must be weighed against harms (https://di.aerzteblatt.de/int/archive/article/231736).

Those harms are real and non-trivial: high rates of false-positive nodule findings requiring follow-up imaging or invasive procedures, some overdiagnosis of indolent cancers, cumulative radiation exposure, and psychological burden of repeated testing (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4978857/).

**Bottom line:** For heavy (ex-)smokers who meet high-risk eligibility criteria (age, pack-years, recency of quitting), regular LDCT screening within a structured program measurably lowers the chance of dying from lung cancer, though it carries a meaningful risk of false positives and overdiagnosis that should be discussed with a clinician before starting screening.
